gallery.title: File:Sana'a.jpg
gallery.description:
According to popular legend, Sana'a was founded by Shem, the son of Noah, not far from the mountain where Noah's ark came to rest when the flood subsided. Yemenis thus claim it to be the oldest living city in the world - upto 10,000 years old, and known to have been inhabited for over 2,500 years. Now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the walled city's 6,500 houses and more than 100 mosques make it a living museum of traditional styles.

It was never easy to reach this "Hidden Jewel of Arabia" which is situated in the heart of mountainous Yemen. Yet those who did manage to complete the dangerous and tiresome journey on donkey or camel-back from the distant coast were awestruck and inspired by the city's tall, beautifully decorated buildings, its well-stocked markets and imposing walls, gates and fortifications.

gallery.title: File:Water crisis in sana'a.jpg
gallery.description: With fuel almost impossible to get hold of in Sanaa, the water authority could not operate the network, so UNICEF worked with the Yemen Petroleum Company to buy fuel and organise water trucking to the most vulnerable parts of Sanaa. We are doing similar work across all parts of the country. Without clean water waterborne diseases are a certainty and put children at risk.

gallery.title: File:Bab-ul-Yemen, Sana'a (2286002741).jpg
gallery.description: The Gate of Yemen is the most important in the medieval wall that surrounds the old city of Sana'a. From this spot, the old city with its tower houses and multiple minarets truly seems right out of a story from the Thousand and One Nights.

gallery.title: File:Tower-Houses in Old Sana'a (صنعاء القديمة) (2286023513).jpg
gallery.description: The medina (old town) of sanaa is a chaotic maze of narrow lanes where time seems to have stopped in the Middle Ages. Tall tower houses with whitewashed window frames and stain glassed windows line the streets that seem to have been thrown with no regard to planning. Occasionally, some larger squares are occupied by orchards and communal vegetable gardens.

gallery.title: File:Vegetable Garden in Old Sana'a (2286045031).jpg
gallery.description: Despite being a city of around 2 million inhabitants, almost every quarter in the medina (old area) of Sana'a has its own community garden where palm trees and vegetables are grown for the benefit of the population. The traditional methods to store irregular rain water have so far been sufficient to sustain the population and irrigate the gardens, but things are changing fast. The poorly effective dams in Yemen are now struggling to supply water for the ever growing population of the city.

(Later we understood there has been a remarkeable and dramatic reversal in the fortunes of the villages on hill tops versus those along roads in the valleys since the 1960s).
